questions.checklist_observation: Are all the following factors considered in the visual inspection program: the condition of the outside of equipment, insulation, painting/coatings, supports and attachments, and identifying mechanical damage, corrosion, vibration, leakage or improper components or repairs?
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Visual inspection checklist, schedule, inspection reports, defect records.
Shopfloor: Verify equipment condition, insulation, coating, supports, corrosion, vibration, leakage, and repairs.
questions.observation:
1. Utility lines, Brine tanks, PB-I Technical area 1st Floor most of the lines and equipments were observed to be corroded 
2. Visual inspection is available for Pressure vessels & Reactors. For auxiliary equipment it is missing like Pipelines, Brine tanks.
3. Cable tray supports rusted and damaged at QC washroom area.
4. I/ST/007 - 5 KL receiver nozzle connected to level indicator is fully corroded at PB-I Day Tank Storage Tank area
5.Insulation is required for the MDC receiver.
6. Street light insulation sleeve damaged and module box corroded in front of QC
questions.recommendations:
1. Carry out a comprehensive corrosion survey of utility lines, brine tanks, pipelines and equipment in the PB-I technical area; repair or replace degraded components, apply a suitable protective coating, and set up regular corrosion monitoring.
2. Extend the written visual-inspection program to all auxiliary equipment, including pipelines, brine tanks, supports, attachments, insulation and coatings, with defined frequency, acceptance criteria and defect-closure tracking.
3. Replace or structurally repair the corroded cable trays and supports at the QC washroom, apply corrosion protection, and inspect the complete cable route for similar deterioration.
4. Remove I/ST/007 from service as required, assess the receiver nozzle and level-indicator connection for remaining thickness and integrity, replace the corroded section, perform a leak test, and return it to service only after competent-person approval.
5. Install chemically and thermally compatible insulation with protective cladding on the MDC receiver and include insulation condition in routine inspections.
6. Replace the damaged street-light insulation sleeve and corroded module box with suitably rated weatherproof components, check electrical insulation and earthing, and put in place regular inspection.

questions.checklist_observation:
As part of the MOC procedure, have the roles and responsibilities of the individuals involved, been clearly defined?

   •  Signing Authority
   •  Subject Matter Expert.

questions.observation: Roles and responsibilities are not defined for MOC team, MOC Coordinator, and approval authorization.
questions.recommendations: Define roles and responsibilities clearly for MOC team, MOC Coordinator, and approval authorization in the procedure as required by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(l).

questions.checklist_observation: Is PHA conducted based on the type of change proposed?
questions.auditor_verification:

questions.observation: Risk assessment is required in EHS Evaluation Form, But the procedure does not specify when which PHA method is required, or vary the depth of PHA according to change type, complexity or risk.
questions.recommendations: Create a risk-based PHA selection matrix that specifies when JSA, What-If, HAZOP or another formal study is required. Record the selected method and justification, participants, recommendations, owners and due dates, and prohibit startup until all pre-startup actions are independently verified closed.

questions.checklist_observation:
Are the effects of change on the workforce, including training requirements, assessed and managed effectively, particularly if the Change affects safety, operational regimes or organizational structure?
Is the same recorded in a Change Register?
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: MOC impact assessment, training need assessment, change register, training/communication records.
Shopfloor: Interview affected employees to confirm awareness and training on change impacts
questions.observation: EHS Evaluation Form asks whether chemical-handling training is needed. But the SOP does not require a written workforce/organizational impact assessment, communication before use, identification of all affected persons, or a controlled MOC register linking training and communication evidence to each change.
questions.recommendations: Add a workforce-impact and communication section to the MOC form covering affected roles, competency changes, training needs, operating-regime changes and organizational impacts. Keep a controlled MOC register and require completed training/communication records before startup or use.

questions.checklist_observation: Is the process safety information (hazards of chemicals, process hazards, process technology and process equipment) updated if changed?
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Updated PSI, P&IDs, chemical/process hazard data, equipment datasheets, MOC closure records.
Shopfloor: Verify updated documents match actual field installation and operating conditions.
questions.observation: PSI procedure is missing just complied using forms, PSI references to be attached to the individual MOC before closure.
questions.recommendations: Prepare and approve a PSI procedure defining document owners, review and update requirements for chemical hazards, process technology, equipment data, P&IDs, design limits and safety systems. For every MOC, identify the affected PSI documents, revise them before startup, check that the documents match the field installation, attach the approved revisions to the MOC and do not close the MOC until the responsible functions confirm completion. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(d), 1910.119(i)(2) and 1910.119(l)(4).

questions.checklist_observation: Are the operating procedures or practices updated if changed?
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Revised SOPs, revision history, MOC linkage, training records.
Shopfloor: Verify current SOPs are available and followed by operators
questions.observation: The SOP does not define how revision control is linked to the MOC, or how affected workers are trained before startup.
questions.recommendations: Require every MOC to identify affected SOPs and safe-work practices, assign a document owner, complete revision/approval through document control, withdraw superseded versions and train affected workers before startup. Record document numbers, revisions and training evidence in the MOC close-out.

questions.checklist_observation: Is the Standard maintenance procedures and maintenance frequency updated as per the accepted change?

questions.checklist_observation: Who validates the Change (for its applicability) and against which criteria (for its applicability/ non-applicability) to move it to the evaluation phase?

questions.observation: The site procedure assigns EHS and the cross-functional team to evaluate proposed changes, and the EHS Head accepts or rejects the change based on criticality. But the procedure does not clearly define written criteria for deciding MOC applicability/non-applicability or require justification and approval for changes screened out of MOC.
questions.recommendations: Add an MOC applicability screening checklist covering replacement-in-kind, changes to chemicals, process conditions, equipment, facilities, software, procedures and organization. Assign the MOC Coordinator with relevant subject-matter experts to validate the screening, record the reason for applicability or non-applicability, and obtain approval before use. Retain screened-out decisions in the MOC register. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(l)(1)-(2).

questions.checklist_observation:

questions.recommendations: Identify Process Safety Critical equipment, assign numbering, and keep list with PM records as required by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j).

questions.observation: Temporary and permanent changes are differention not mnetioned clearly in the MOC procedure
questions.recommendations: Clearly define and differentiate temporary and permanent changes in the MOC procedure as required by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(l).

questions.recommendations: Identify Process Safety Critical equipment, assign numbering, and keep list with PM records as required by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j).

questions.checklist_observation: Is there review system for effecting any change in the existing plant, equipment or process? Give details of changes or new equipment review (P&I diagram, HAZOP studies, Risk assessment and other documents)
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: MOC records, P&ID review, HAZOP/PHA, risk assessment, design documents, approval records, action tracker.
Shopfloor: Verify changed equipment/process matches approved documents and actions are closed before operation.
questions.observation: The site procedure provides EHS and cross-functional review of proposed changes and requires PSSR where applicable. But it does not clearly require every plant, equipment or process change to include the applicable updated P&ID, HAZOP/PHA or risk assessment, approved design documents, action-closure evidence and field check before use or startup.
questions.recommendations: Add a document checklist and close-out gate to every MOC. Based on the change, attach the approved P&ID, design documents, HAZOP/PHA or risk assessment, equipment specifications and action tracker. Before startup, check the installation against the approved documents, close all pre-startup actions, update affected PSI and procedures, and obtain authorization from Engineering, Operations and EHS. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(l)(1)-(2), 1910.119(i)(2) and 1910.119(d).

questions.checklist_observation: Does the facility have a PSSR procedure that covers new installations, temporary shutdowns, maintenance turnarounds, and extended shutdowns, with or without modifications?

Shopfloor: Verify PSSR implementation before start-up/restart and operator awareness.
questions.observation: Site procedure is available but it does not clearly list temporary shutdowns, maintenance turnarounds, extended shutdowns, or restarts without a modification as PSSR triggers.
questions.recommendations: Revise site procedure to include a simple PSSR trigger table covering: new facilities; significant modifications; major turnarounds; and restart after temporary or extended shutdown where equipment condition, safeguards, procedures or operating readiness may have changed. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(i)(1) and 1910.119(i)(2).

questions.checklist_observation: A written report has been prepared for each safety review performed for a new covered process.

questions.recommendations: Require a controlled PSSR report for every applicable review, including a unique reference number, supporting evidence, action status, approvals and other requirements.

questions.checklist_observation:
The safety review design report has included the following:
a) The date of the report and an identification of the covered process, the process safety information, and standard operating procedures reviewed
b) An identification of the codes and standards upon which the covered process design and operations were based
c) The names of the persons who performed the safety review
d) The deviations from the design and operating codes and standards that were found with an appropriate description of the resolution of each
questions.auditor_verification:
a) Document: PSSR report with date, process identification, PSI/SOP review records.
Shopfloor: Verify updated SOPs, process information, and operator access.
b)Document: Design basis, applicable codes/standards, drawings, equipment specifications.

c)Document: PSSR team list, attendance sheet, sign-off/approval records.
Shopfloor: Interview team members/operators on participation and start-up conditions.
d)Document: Deviation register, risk assessment, MOC, approval records, action closure evidence.
Shopfloor: Verify deviation controls implemented and no critical open deviations.
questions.observation: Site procedure does not clearly require a single report to list all applicable codes/standards, all deviations found and how each deviation was resolved.
questions.recommendations: Add a mandatory report section for the review date; process/equipment identification; PSI and procedures reviewed; applicable design codes and standards; PSSR team names and functions; deviations found; risk/temporary controls; action owner and due date; and evidence of final resolution. Do not authorize startup with unresolved pre-startup actions. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(i)(2)(i)-(iv)

questions.checklist_observation: PSSRs have been performed for new facilities.

questions.recommendations: Add a written PSSR screening step to every MOC. If the modification changes PSI, design limits, equipment, controls, chemicals, procedures or safeguards, complete and approve the PSSR before introducing hazardous chemicals or restarting the process. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(i)(1), 1910.119(i)(2)(iii) and 1910.119(l).

questions.checklist_observation: Is there personnel available for managing, scheduling PSSR in the unit?

questions.recommendations: Designate workers for managing and scheduling PSSR activities as required by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(i).

questions.checklist_observation: PSSRs have confirmed that training of each employee involved in operating a modified process has been completed.

But the SOP does not state that every operator affected by a modified process must complete and document the required training before startup authorization.
questions.recommendations: Make training completion a mandatory startup gate. Prepare an affected-person list, train each operator on revised hazards, operating steps, limits, alarms/interlocks and emergency actions, assess understanding, update training records and check completion on the PSSR before authorization. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(i)(2)(iv), 1910.119(g), and 1910.119(l)(3).

questions.checklist_observation: Decisions and actions resulting from the PSSR are communicated to appropriate personnel

questions.recommendations: Add a communication record to the PSSR file. Before startup, brief affected operations, maintenance and contractor workers on the approved change, operating limits, hazards, safeguards and emergency actions; assign owners for any approved post-startup actions and obtain attendance/acknowledgement. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(l)(3), supported by 1910.119(g) for operating workers and 1910.119(h) for contractors.

questions.observation:

questions.checklist_observation: Do workers follow safe procedures for storage of materials?

questions.observation:
• Iso Propyl Acetate (Flash Point -2◦C) & Acetonitrile  (Flash Point -2◦C),N-Heptane solvent drums were stored in solvent road tanker unloading area and on outside roads. 
•Improper segregation of stored pipelines / hoses observed at solvent yard.

• Material stacking was not good in the Intermediate Material Storage room at PB-II

questions.recommendations:

• Replace non-standard plastic pallets with approved load-rated and chemical-resistant pallets. Remove damaged or unsuitable pallets from use.
• Restack materials in the PB-II Intermediate Material Storage Room within the approved height and load limits. Use stable pallets or racks and keep all aisles clear.
• Include these storage conditions in the daily area inspection checklist and correct any unsafe condition immediately.
• Provide Flame proof cabinets for Solvent storage in QC.

questions.observation:
Ambulance related issues 
-First Aid box in ambulance has no ID & contents label
-Expired medicines (Pantodex injection expired in June'2026) was observed in Ambulance First aid box 
-Ambulance driver, was not available in the vehicle - he came after 30 Min. 
-Ambulance - Insurance got expired in May'2026, Fitness & Road tax certificate (expired in 2019) not available 
-Ambulance driver - First aid training certificate not available 
-Training & Expereince records of ambulance driver not available 
-Ambulance siren needs to be relocated, right know it is near to tyres. 
-Ambulance door and latches damaged and pending repair for more than one month.
-No communication record available for reported ambulance issues, fuel, and speedometer concerns.
-The due date of fire extinguisher servicing in the ambulance has expired.
-Ambulance vehicle condition check was not carried out by the driver; it was done by the paramedic."
questions.recommendations:
-Provide durable, clearly visible identification and safety labels at the point of use, and add label condition and legibility to routine inspections.
-Immediately remove and safely dispose of expired medical items, replenish approved stock, and implement a documented monthly expiry check with accountable sign-off.
-Provide a dedicated trained ambulance driver for every shift, maintain a duty roster and backup arrangement, and verify response readiness through periodic drills.
-Renew the ambulance insurance, fitness certificate and road tax before further use, and maintain a compliance tracker with advance renewal alerts.
-Ensure the ambulance driver completes approved first-aid training and retain a valid certificate with refresher due-date tracking.
-Verify the driver's competency and experience, compile the required records, and maintain them in the ambulance personnel file with periodic review.
-Relocate the siren to a protected position that provides effective audible coverage and is not exposed to wheel or road damage; function-test it after installation.
-Repair the ambulance door and latches immediately, prohibit service if secure closure is affected, and close the maintenance request with a functional check.
-Create a defect-reporting and escalation log for ambulance issues, including owner, target date, closure evidence and verification before each shift.
-Remove or replace the overdue extinguisher immediately, complete servicing by an authorized agency, and add advance due-date alerts to the inspection register.
-Assign the ambulance driver responsibility for the pre-use vehicle condition check, train the driver on the checklist, and require signed verification before each shift.

questions.checklist_observation: Whether the emergency siren audibility being check at various areas? Whether records being maintained?
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Emergency Siren testing records.

questions.recommendations: Set up monthly electrical and manual siren tests from representative high-noise, remote and occupied areas. Define an audibility criterion, record results, correct weak coverage.

questions.checklist_observation: Is there a written incident reporting & investigation procedure in place that describes the management systems to address how incident investigations are to be organized, staffed, managed, documented, reported, and how the follow-up is to be performed
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Incident reporting & investigation SOP, approval, revision history.  
Shopfloor: Ask EHS team to explain investigation workflow.
questions.observation: The site procedure does not define how incident investigations are to be organized, staffed, managed, written, formally reported, followed up, and closed.
questions.recommendations: Prepare and use a formal Incident Reporting & Investigation Management System defining investigation team structure, roles and responsibilities, records, reporting, CAPA tracking, and closure requirements as required by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(m) and ISO 45001:2018 Clause 10.2.

questions.checklist_observation: Is there a procedure or process in place to internally report all incidents including near misses so that formal investigations can be initiated promptly, as appropriate
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Incident reporting procedure, reporting forms.  
Shopfloor: Ask employees how to report near misses.
questions.observation: Incident reporting & Investigation Procedure is available and employees are being trained on the procedure.

questions.checklist_observation: Does the procedure covers the guidance for evidence collection and responsible authorities
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: SOP section for evidence handling (photos, samples, witness).  
Shopfloor: Ask investigators about evidence collection steps.
questions.observation: The site procedure does not provide detailed requirements for identifying, collecting, documenting, handling, preserving, and storing physical, documentary, or electronic evidence, or define the responsible authorities.
questions.recommendations:
Update the incident investigation procedure to include detailed guidance on: 
(a) Identification of evidence types (physical, documentary, electronic), 
(b) records using photographs, sketches, and written records, 
(c) Proper handling and storage of evidence. 
Refer OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 for evidence management requirements.

questions.checklist_observation: Does the procedure classify Process safety events in line with API 754 or other relevant standards?
questions.auditor_verification: Document: Incident classification matrix (Tier 1–4 etc.).  Shopfloor: Verify classification of recent incidents.
questions.observation: The site procedure does not include Process Safety Event classification as required by API RP 754 Tier 1, Tier 2, Tier 3, and Tier 4 criteria.
questions.recommendations:
Revise incident classification procedure to include API RP 754 process safety metrics:
A) Tier 1 - Primary containment loss with serious consequences
B) Tier 2 - Primary containment loss with lesser consequences
C) Tier 3 - Near misses and challenges to safety systems
D) Tier 4 - Operating discipline and management system indicators
Refer to API RP 754:2016 and OISD-STD-154.

questions.checklist_observation:
Does the organization establish, implement and maintain a procedure(s) for dealing with Process safety Events and for taking corrective action and preventive action. The procedure(s) shall define requirements for: 
a) identifying and correcting nonconformity(is) and taking action(s) to mitigate their environmental impacts
b) investigating nonconformity(is), determining their cause(s) and taking actions in order to avoid their recurrence,
c) evaluating the need for action(s) to prevent nonconformity(is) and implementing appropriate actions designed to avoid their occurrence, 
d) recording the results of corrective action(s) and preventive action(s) taken, and 
e) reviewing the effectiveness of corrective action(s) and preventive action(s) taken.
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: CAPA procedure / integrated module.  
Shopfloor: Check understanding of CAPA closure process.
questions.observation: The site procedure does not include requirements for Process Safety Event classification, investigation, corrective and preventive action tracking, recording of results, and effectiveness review.
questions.recommendations: Update the incident reporting & investigation procedure to include API RP 754 Process Safety Event (Tier 1–4) classification, investigation requirements, CAPA tracking, and effectiveness review for process safety incidents.

questions.checklist_observation: Does the procedure require that the  investigation team  include

questions.observation: The site procedure mentions investigation-team composition, but does not define competency requirements for the team leader and members or the authority responsible for constituting and approving the investigation committee.
questions.recommendations: Define the competency requirements for investigation team leaders and members and clearly specify the authority responsible for constituting and approving investigation committees based on incident severity, as required by OSHA PSM 29 CFR 1910.119(m) and ISO 45001 Clauses 7.2 & 10.2.

questions.checklist_observation: a. Team composition for type of Incidents / Accidents

c. Authority for constitution of investigation committee

questions.checklist_observation: a. date of incident

f. Recommendation to prevent recurrence
Does the Incident element procedure define the levels of investigation based on its Risk and consequence. ( RCA/ ACA/ External investigation)
questions.auditor_verification:

questions.observation: The site procedure does not define risk- and consequence-based investigation levels or criteria for RCA, ACA, cross-functional team, and external investigations.
questions.recommendations: Define investigation levels based on risk and consequence severity, including requirements for investigation scope, team composition, approval authority, and RCA methodology as required by OSHA PSM 29 CFR 1910.119(m) and ISO 45001:2018 Clause 10.2

questions.checklist_observation: Has each incident been investigated which resulted in, or could have reasonable resulted in a catastrophic release of a regulated substance?
questions.auditor_verification:

Shopfloor: Cross-check major incidents vs investigation reports
questions.observation: The site procedure does not explicitly mandate investigation of incidents that resulted in, or could reasonably have resulted in, a catastrophic release of a regulated substance.
questions.recommendations: Revise the procedure to mandate investigation of incidents that caused or could have caused a catastrophic release, including prompt RCA, CAPA tracking, effectiveness review, and closure, as required by OSHA PSM 29 CFR 1910.119(m).

questions.checklist_observation: Have incident investigations been initiated as promptly as possible, but not later than 48 hours following the incident?

Document: Incident timestamps vs investigation start date.  
Shopfloor: Verify prompt response practices.

questions.checklist_observation: Do the teams contain at least one person knowledgeable in the process involved in the incident, and other members with appropriate knowledge and experience to thoroughly investigate and analyse the incident?
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Investigation team composition records.  
Shopfloor: Verify involvement of relevant department experts.

questions.checklist_observation: Have resolutions and corrective actions from the incident investigation reports been documented?
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Incident report with actions.  
Shopfloor: Verify action clarity and feasibility.

questions.checklist_observation: Are the Incident investigation reports are issued promptly on completion of the investigation?
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Report issue date vs investigation completion.  
Shopfloor: Ask stakeholders about reporting timelines.
questions.observation: The site procedure does not define formal timelines, controlled issuance, distribution, acknowledgement, and document-control requirements for completed investigation reports.
questions.recommendations: Set up a formal report issuance system with: (a) Defined timelines for report completion and distribution, (b) Official circulation to all affected departments, (c) Acknowledgment receipt from stakeholders, (d) Document control number for tracking. Refer to Factories Act 1948 Section 88A, OISD-GDN-206, and IS 14489:2018 for incident reporting requirements.

questions.checklist_observation: Have incident investigation reports been reviewed with affected employees whose job tasks are relevant to the incident findings including contract employees, wherever applicable?
questions.auditor_verification:

Shopfloor: Ask employees about recent incident learnings
questions.observation: The site procedure does not require written review of investigation findings with affected employees and contractors or retention of their acknowledgement records.
questions.recommendations: Set up a system to communicate incident investigation findings to affected employees and contractors and keep records of such reviews for check and follow-up as required by OSHA PSM 29 CFR 1910.119(m) and ISO 45001:2018 Clause 10.2

questions.checklist_observation: Do the Employees have access to incident investigation reports?
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Incident reports, safety alerts,  training/toolbox talk records.
Shopfloor: Interview employees for access and awareness of incident learnings.
questions.observation: The site procedure does not define a formal mechanism for providing employees and relevant stakeholders access to issued incident-investigation reports.
questions.recommendations: Set up a formal report issuance system with: (a) Defined timelines for report completion and distribution, (b) Official circulation to all affected departments, (c) Acknowledgment receipt from stakeholders. Refer to Factories Act 1948 Section 88A, OISD-GDN-206, and IS 14489:2018 for incident reporting requirements.

questions.checklist_observation:

questions.observation: Universal CAPA Tracker system is  available

questions.auditor_verification:

Shopfloor: Interview lead investigators on RCA, evidence collection, and CAPA development
questions.observation: The site procedure does not define RCA training, competency assessment, certification, and refresher requirements or records for lead investigators.
questions.recommendations: Provide formal RCA training to all lead investigators covering: (a) 5-Why Analysis, (b) Fishbone/Ishikawa Diagram, (c) Fault Tree Analysis, keep training records with certificates, competency assessment, and refresher schedules. Refer to OISD-GDN-206, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119, and IS 14489:2018 for investigator competency requirements.

questions.checklist_observation: Are the company employees trained on Incident reporting procedures

Document: Incident reporting SOP, induction/refresher training records, reporting formats.
Shopfloor: Interview employees on what, when, whom, and how to report incidents.
questions.observation: Employees are being trained.
questions.recommendations: Make sure employees are trained on incident reporting procedures and keep training records as evidence of competency and awareness as required by ISO 45001:2018 Clause 7.2, Clause 7.3 and OSHA PSM 29 CFR 1910.119(g).

questions.checklist_observation: Does the investigation team members trained on Investigation procedures and methodology
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Investigation procedure, team training records, nomination records, RCA templates.
Shopfloor: Interview team members on scene preservation, evidence collection, and investigation methodology.
questions.observation: The site procedure does not define written training and competency requirements for investigation-team members on investigation procedures and methodologies.
questions.recommendations: Make sure investigation team members are trained on incident investigation methodologies and keep written training records to demonstrate competency as required by ISO 45001:2018 Clause 7.2and OSHA PSM 29 CFR 1910.119(g).

questions.checklist_observation: Do the employees communicated on Incident causes and recommendations
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Safety alerts, incident learning sheets, flash presentations, communication and attendance records.
Shopfloor: Verify employee awareness of incident causes, recommendations, and preventive actions.
questions.observation: Incident causes, recommendations, and lessons learned are communicated.

questions.checklist_observation: Are incidents (including near‑catastrophic chemical release scenarios) investigated, with lessons learned documented, communicated through training flash presentations, and distributed across all company locations?”
questions.auditor_verification:
Document: Investigation reports, lessons learned, flash presentations, cross-site communication records, CAPA tracker.
Shopfloor: Verify implementation of learnings and employee awareness of emergency/chemical release response actions.
questions.observation: Lessons learned from incidents including near-miss chemical release scenarios are written but not consistently communicated across all company locations through training flash presentations.
questions.recommendations: Put in place a structured lessons learned sharing system: (a) Prepare one-page safety alerts for each significant incident, (b) Distribute flash presentations to all company locations within 7 days, (c) carry out toolbox talks and awareness sessions, (d) keep acknowledgment records from all locations. Refer to OISD-GDN-206, Factories Act 1948 Section 41B, and OSHA PSM guidelines for cross-site communication requirements.

questions.checklist_observation: Does the company carry out analysis of accidents, based on different criteria, and effectively communicate the findings of the same with its personnel?

Make sure the investigation identifies main hazards, system deficiencies, and corrective steps as required by ISO 45001:2018 Clause 10.2 and OSHA incident investigation guidance

Policy display boards across plant.

Observe leadership involvement in shopfloor activities.

Lesson learned documents shared.

RCA reports, CAPA tracker.

questions.checklist_observation: Employees/staff and Leadership team reward good safety performance and identify learning to leverage across the site/company.

Annual report EHS section.

questions.checklist_observation:
Does the OHC have the following –
• Facilities available to handle emergency cases and provide first aid
• Ambulance permanently stationed at the facility with all amenities
• Bed space available (as per Factories Act)
questions.auditor_verification:
Document:
Emergency facility checklist, ambulance fitness documents.
Shopfloor:
Check availability of beds, first‑aid equipment, working ambulance.
questions.observation:
1) Medicine inventory and stock levels are not being adequately maintained in the occupational health center. Essential medicines may be unavailable or expired when needed. Establish minimum and maximum stock levels, expiry tracking, storage-condition checks, periodic inventory review, and documented replenishment responsibilities.

2) A current list of hazardous chemicals used or stored at the site is not available in the occupational health center. Medical personnel may lack critical information for exposure assessment and treatment. Maintain an updated chemical inventory with SDS access, hazard classification, likely exposure routes, and emergency treatment guidance.

3) Inventory records for medical materials and consumables were not being maintained. Lack of stock management may result in shortages of critical medical supplies during emergencies.

4) List of hazardous chemicals handled at the site was not available in the OHC. Absence of this information may delay appropriate medical treatment during chemical exposure incidents.

5) Oxygen cylinder was last filled in 2024 and no evidence of annual refilling was available. Lack of periodic refilling may affect oxygen availability during medical emergencies.

6) Spare oxygen cylinder trolley was not available in the OHC. Absence of a trolley may delay transportation and deployment of oxygen cylinders during emergencies.

7) Dedicated ambulance driver was not available for emergency transportation. Non-availability of a trained ambulance driver may result in delays in medical evacuation and emergency response.
questions.recommendations:
1) Implement a controlled medical inventory system with item codes, minimum/maximum levels, batch and expiry tracking, storage-condition monitoring, periodic reconciliation, and replenishment responsibilities. Quarantine expired or damaged stock and document disposal.

2) Maintain a controlled, current hazardous-chemical inventory in the OHC linked to approved SDS, exposure routes, symptoms, first-aid measures, antidote requirements, and emergency contacts. Establish change notification from procurement, production, and EHS and review the list periodically.

3) Implement an item-wise inventory register for medicines and consumables with minimum/maximum stock, batch, expiry, storage conditions, issue, and replenishment tracking. Perform periodic reconciliation and quarantine expired or damaged materials.

4) Maintain a controlled hazardous-chemical list in the OHC linked to current SDS, exposure routes, symptoms, first aid, antidotes, and emergency contacts. Require EHS notification for additions or changes and review the list at a defined frequency.

5) Have the oxygen cylinder inspected, pressure and contents verified, and refilled or replaced by an authorized agency before emergency use. Establish cylinder identification, fill and hydro-test tracking, minimum reserve quantity, routine pressure checks, and expiry alerts.

6) Provide a compatible, stable oxygen-cylinder trolley with secure restraints and wheels suitable for emergency movement. Keep it accessible, inspect it routinely, and train OHC staff in safe cylinder handling and transport.

7) Provide continuous emergency transport coverage through a dedicated trained ambulance driver or a documented roster with competent backups. Define response-time expectations, verify licences and fitness, test call-out arrangements, and record drill performance.

questions.observation:
1) The preventive maintenance procedure for gas detectors in all areas does not specify the required inspection, calibration, and testing frequency. This may result in overdue maintenance and unreliable detector performance during an emergency. Revise the procedure to define responsibilities, frequencies, acceptance criteria, records, and actions for failed detectors.

2) Three LEL (Lower Explosive Limit) detectors were found in trouble/fault condition. Non-functional gas detection systems may prevent timely detection of flammable gas leaks, increasing the risk of fire, explosion, and unsafe operating conditions.
questions.recommendations:
1) Revise and approve the gas-detector preventive-maintenance procedure to specify equipment-wise inspection, bump-test, calibration, functional-test frequencies, acceptance criteria, responsibilities, records, and actions for failed or overdue detectors. Track due dates and escalate exceptions before continued operation.

2) Treat the affected areas as unmonitored until the three LEL detectors are restored. Repair, calibrate, bump-test, and function-test each detector; provide temporary monitoring or stop hazardous work, investigate common-cause failure, and retain service and alarm-verification records.

questions.observation:
1) Steam line leakages were observed at multiple locations. Leakage from steam lines can result in energy loss, reduced system efficiency, and potential burn hazards to personnel working in the vicinity.

2) Leakage is present at flanges and pump seals in the hot-oil system. Escaping hot oil can cause burns, slips, fire, and equipment damage.

3) Pump seal leakages and pipeline flange leakages were observed in the boiler area. The identified leakages may result in loss of utility media, reduced system efficiency, housekeeping issues, and increased risk of personnel exposure to hot fluids or steam.
questions.recommendations:
1) Identify, isolate, and repair all steam leaks using an approved leak register and priority based on pressure, temperature, and personnel exposure. Replace defective traps, gaskets, valves, or insulation as applicable, barricade hazardous locations, and verify leak-free restoration.

2) Isolate and repair the leaking points, inspect gaskets and seals, clean contaminated surfaces, and implement periodic leak checks and preventive maintenance.

3) Identify, isolate, and repair all pump-seal and flange leaks using compatible seals and gaskets. Barricade hot-fluid exposure areas, clean contamination, verify leak-free restoration under operating conditions, and establish routine leak inspections and failure trending.

2) Preventive maintenance records or status labels are not available for the hydraulic trolleys. Defects affecting brakes, wheels, hydraulics, or load stability may therefore remain undetected.

questions.observation:
1) Centrifuge wet material is being stored on the walkways at both the ground floor and first floor of Production Block-1. This obstructs safe access and egress routes, creates housekeeping issues, and increases the risk of slips, trips, falls, and emergency evacuation difficulties.

2) Methocarbomol material from centrifuge is being stored on the walkways at the ground floor of Production Block-5. This obstructs safe access and egress routes, creates housekeeping issues, and increases the risk of slips, trips, falls, and emergency evacuation difficulties.

3) The front side of the HR Office was found blocked with finished materials. Obstruction of access and movement areas may affect safe pedestrian movement, hinder emergency evacuation, and impact overall housekeeping standards.

3) Remove finished materials from the HR Office frontage and restore the designated pedestrian and emergency-access route. Mark a no-storage zone, provide an approved alternate storage location, and include access clearance in daily housekeeping inspections.

questions.observation:
1) Damaged pallets are being used for material storage in the warehouse, and material stacking practices are inadequate. Engineering warehouse materials are stored improperly, creating potential safety hazards. Damaged pallets should be replaced, and proper storage and stacking procedures should be implemented to ensure safe and organized material handling.

2) 1st crop material was found stagnated on the ground floor and first floor of Block-I. Accumulation of material in production areas may affect housekeeping standards, obstruct movement, and increase the risk of material mix-up or process inefficiencies.

3) A large quantity of finished goods is stored directly on the floor in FG stores 1, 2, and 3. This may obstruct cleaning and access, and create unstable stacking or manual-handling hazards. Store materials on sound pallets or racks with defined aisles, stacking limits, and location identification.

4) Four batches of first-crop material are stored directly on the floor in block-1. This can cause contamination or damage, obstruct movement and cleaning, and create manual-handling and housekeeping hazards.
questions.recommendations:
1) Remove damaged pallets from service and replace them with load-rated pallets or racks. Define stacking height and load limits, maintain clear aisles, identify storage locations, and implement documented pallet and housekeeping inspections.

2) Transfer first-crop material to identified pallets or racks in a designated status-controlled area. Define maximum holding time, quantity limits, ownership, and disposal or processing actions; keep aisles clear and verify compliance through daily housekeeping inspections.

3) Transfer finished goods from the floor to load-rated pallets or racks in designated locations. Define stacking and rack-load limits, maintain marked aisles and fire-system clearances, inspect pallet condition, and include floor-storage prohibition in warehouse checks.

4) Transfer the material to identified pallets or racks in a designated area and maintain clear aisles and status labelling.

questions.checklist_observation: Whether methodology for handling spillages of hazardous chemical available along with the equipment required handling the spillage?
questions.auditor_verification:

questions.observation:
1) Spill Control Kits were not provided with unique identification numbering, and the corresponding SOP for spill kit management and usage was not available. This may lead to ineffective inventory control, delayed spill response, and improper utilization of spill response materials during emergency situations.

2) Spill control kit was not available in the scrap yard area. Absence of spill response equipment may delay the containment and cleanup of oil, fuel, or chemical spills, increasing the risk of environmental contamination, fire hazards, and unsafe working conditions.

3) Spill control kit was not available at the DG Set diesel storage area. Absence of spill response equipment may delay containment and cleanup of diesel spills, increasing the risk of soil contamination, fire hazards, and unsafe working conditions.
questions.recommendations:
1) Assign a unique ID to every spill kit and issue an approved SOP covering contents, location, inspection frequency, replenishment, use, waste disposal, and escalation. Maintain a master register and seal or tag each kit after inspection.

2) Provide a uniquely identified spill kit sized and equipped for credible scrap-yard oil, fuel, and chemical spills. Define inspection and replenishment requirements, train users, display response instructions, and ensure collected waste is managed through the approved disposal route.

3) Provide a uniquely identified diesel-compatible spill kit at the DG-set storage area with absorbents, drain protection, PPE, waste bags, and response instructions. Inspect and replenish it routinely, train users, and link spill waste to the approved disposal process.

questions.observation:

2) DCDA is being charged manually into reactors SSR-101-01, SSR-102-01, SSR-103-01, and SSR-104-01 in block-1. Manual charging may expose operators to chemical contact, dust or vapor release, and ergonomic hazards.

3) A mobile phone deposit box is not provided outside the tank farm area. Personnel may carry non-certified electronic devices into a hazardous area, creating a potential ignition source.

4) A mobile phone deposit box is not provided outside the warehouse controlled area. Personnel may carry prohibited electronic devices into locations where flammable materials are stored or dispensed.
questions.recommendations:
1) Provide a closed charging arrangement with dust extraction, earthing, suitable PPE, and an approved operating procedure.

2) Implement a closed or mechanized charging system supported by risk assessment, local exhaust ventilation, earthing, and appropriate PPE.

3) Install a secure, clearly labelled deposit box before the controlled-area entrance and enforce the restriction through signage and access checks.

questions.observation:
1) Cleanroom garment static electricity checking procedure was not available. Absence of a documented procedure for monitoring and verifying static charge on cleanroom garments may increase the risk of electrostatic discharge, potentially affecting product quality and process safety.

2) A procedure is not available for inspecting and testing the static touch pad. A defective touch pad may not dissipate personnel static charge before entry into a hazardous area.

2) Establish a documented checking frequency, acceptance criteria, records, defect reporting, and prompt repair arrangements.

3) Provide approved conductive or static-safe containers, bonding and earthing, ventilation, spill containment, and controlled transfer methods.

Shopfloor: Verify PPE usage at workplaces, check availability and condition of PPE, and interview employees on PPE requirements, usage, and consequences of non-compliance.
questions.observation:
1) The PPE box at the entrance to Block-3 was being used to store clothing instead of the required personal protective equipment. Required PPE may therefore be unavailable when personnel enter the area or respond to an incident.

2) It was observed that a PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) Matrix was not available in the area. In the absence of a defined PPE Matrix, personnel may not have clear guidance on the specific PPE requirements for various tasks and work areas.

3) PPE Box identification numbering and item inspection/checking procedure were not available in Scrap Yard. Absence of unique identification and a defined inspection procedure may result in ineffective monitoring of PPE availability, condition, and replenishment, potentially affecting emergency preparedness and personnel safety.

4) Employees and contract workmen in the QC laboratory were observed performing analysis activities without wearing the required PPE, including safety goggles, nose masks, and gloves. Non-compliance with PPE requirements may increase the risk of exposure to chemical splashes, vapors, dust, and other occupational health hazards during laboratory operations.
questions.recommendations:
1) Remove unrelated items, replenish the specified PPE, label the box, and assign routine inventory checks.

2) Develop an area- and task-specific PPE matrix from risk assessments and SDS requirements, defining mandatory PPE, standards, limitations, replacement criteria, and exceptions. Display the controlled matrix, train users, and audit compliance routinely.

3) Assign unique IDs to all PPE boxes and issue a checklist defining required contents, condition, quantity, expiry, inspection frequency, replenishment, and responsibility. Seal or tag completed inspections and retain records for review.

4) Stop the affected QC laboratory activities until required PPE is worn. Reinforce the task-specific PPE matrix and SDS requirements, ensure adequate PPE availability and fit, train employees and contractors, implement supervisor pre-start checks, and record and escalate repeated violations.

questions.observation:

questions.observation:
1) Diesel storage drums located near the powerhouse are maintained without adequate secondary containment. In addition, the identification tag affixed to a full diesel drum incorrectly indicates that the drum is empty.

2) Hydrochloric acid (HCl) and isopropyl alcohol (IPA) are stored within the production block-3 without secondary containment. A leak or spill could spread into work areas, causing chemical exposure, environmental contamination, and fire risk in the case of IPA.

3) Warehouse liquid storage drums lack secondary containment. Provide self-contained spill containment pallets to prevent spills, enhance workplace safety, and protect the environment.

4) Dimethyl carbonate is stored or handled without secondary containment. A leak or spill could spread to surrounding areas and generate flammable vapor.

5) Chemical drums in the warehouse are not consistently placed on self-contained spill pallets. Leakage could spread across the floor, expose personnel, and mix with incompatible materials.

6) Biodiesel drums are stored without self-contained spill pallets infront of warehouse. A leak could spread to surrounding areas and create slip, environmental, and fire hazards.
questions.recommendations:
1) Place all diesel drums in a designated, protected storage area with compatible secondary containment sized for the credible spill. Correct the status label immediately and implement container identification, inventory reconciliation, inspection, and segregation controls.

2) Provide compatible, adequately sized spill-containment pallets and segregate incompatible chemicals.

3) Place all liquid drums on compatible, load-rated spill-containment pallets sized for the credible release. Maintain segregation, closure, labels, aisle clearance, and routine documented inspection; remove leaking containers from service immediately.

4) Provide a compatible spill-containment pallet of adequate capacity and ensure containers remain closed, labelled, and protected from ignition sources.

5) Provide compatible containment pallets of adequate capacity for all drums and maintain chemical segregation and inspection controls.

6) Place the drums on compatible secondary containment of adequate capacity and maintain proper labelling, segregation, and inspection.

questions.observation:
1) Near BD/SSR-104-01 in block-1, a plastic drum is covered with a plastic sheet and exposed to a high-temperature environment. Exposure to elevated temperatures may cause deterioration of the drum and cover, potentially leading to material degradation, leakage, pressure build-up, or fire hazards depending on the contents stored.

2) Approximately 3 tonnes of Methocarbon material was found stored at the rear side of the gate under a tarpaulin cover. Storage of material in an undesignated outdoor location may lead to deterioration of material quality, environmental exposure, housekeeping concerns, and potential safety risks.

3) Flammable solvent drums are being stored open and exposed to direct sunlight in the open area near the lift at Block-III. Heat exposure and open containers can increase vapor generation, spillage, and fire risk.

4) Limit storage to the required 2 drums at the point of use and relocate the remaining drums to a designated fuel storage area.

5) A diesel-filled drum is stored in front of the engineering store. The location lacks appropriate control and may expose the drum to impact, leakage, ignition sources, or obstruction of access.
questions.recommendations:
1) Identify the drum contents and relocate it away from heat to a compatible, designated storage area with suitable containment and ventilation. Confirm container material compatibility and temperature limits from the approved SDS, replace degraded packaging, and prohibit temporary plastic-sheet covers.

2) Move the approximately 3 tonnes of material to an approved covered warehouse or engineered temporary storage area with pallets, weather protection, drainage control, identification, and inventory status. Assess material quality before use and prohibit storage near gates or emergency access routes.

3) Keep the drums closed and relocate them to a shaded, ventilated, designated flammable-liquid storage area with secondary containment.

4) Ensure proper stacking, secondary containment, and maintain clear, unobstructed walkways in accordance with industrial safety requirements.

5) Relocate it to a designated fuel storage area with secondary containment, identification, segregation, and firefighting provisions.

1) Vent condensers were not available for the storage tanks in the tank farm area. Absence of vent condensers may lead to increased solvent vapor emissions, product loss, and potential environmental and safety concerns during tank breathing operations.

questions.observation:
1) During the transfer of Toluene/Methanol from the storage tank to the day tank, a fixed transfer set point of 500 L is used. As the day tank may already contain material, there is a potential risk of overfilling, leading to spills, vapor release, and fire hazards.

2) Overflow protection is not available for solvent transfer from the tank farm to the production blocks. A receiving vessel could be overfilled, causing spills, vapor release, and fire. Install independent high-level alarms and automatic transfer shutdown interlocks, and verify their operation through periodic proof testing.
questions.recommendations:
1) Install level measurement with independent high-level and high-high alarms and automatic transfer shutdown. Calculate the permissible transfer quantity from verified receiving-tank ullage rather than a fixed volume, require pre-transfer confirmation, and proof-test the interlocks periodically.

2) Install independent high-level and high-high protection on each receiving vessel, with automatic pump or valve shutdown and alarm annunciation. Define proof-test frequency and bypass control, record test results, and prohibit transfer when protection is unavailable.

questions.checklist_observation: Does Plant has identified & eliminated all Open handling activities of solvents for cleaning equipment, equipment parts and accessories in process areas and WH

Document: Solvent handling SOP, closed cleaning/transfer procedure, risk assessment, improvement records.
Shopfloor: Verify no open solvent handling, closed transfer systems, proper containers, ventilation, and ignition source control.
questions.observation:
1) Recovered toluene generated after distillation is being transferred in drums from block-3. Open or manual drum transfer can lead to spills, vapor exposure, static discharge, and fire.

2) Sodium methoxide is being mixed with methanol in an open stainless-steel container during solution preparation in block-5. Open handling may release flammable methanol vapors and expose personnel to a highly reactive chemical, creating fire and contact hazards.

3) Methanol is being used for utensil cleaning without a documented justification or approved risk assessment. Its high flammability and toxicity may expose personnel to unnecessary vapor, fire, and skin-contact hazards.

4) PCF unloading is being performed in an open condition in block-1. This may expose personnel to dust, vapors, splashes, and uncontrolled material release. Provide a closed unloading arrangement with suitable extraction or containment, earthing where required, appropriate PPE, and a documented procedure.
questions.recommendations:
1) Replace open drum transfer with a closed, bonded and earthed transfer system using compatible piping, pumps, hoses, dry-break couplings, vapor control, and secondary containment. Define transfer limits, pre-transfer checks, spill response, and inspection requirements.

2) Replace open mixing with a closed, inerted and bonded system designed for sodium methoxide and methanol compatibility. Provide controlled addition, ventilation, temperature monitoring, spill containment, emergency isolation, and an approved operating procedure based on reaction-risk assessment.

3) Evaluate safer substitutes and, if methanol remains necessary, define closed handling, ventilation, PPE, storage, and waste controls in an approved procedure.

4) Provide a closed PCF unloading system with compatible connections, local extraction or containment, bonding/earthing where required, and spill control. Validate performance, define pre-use checks and PPE, train operators, and document the unloading procedure.

questions.observation:
1) The earth plate at the GFN spent mixed solvent unloading area was found in a rusted condition near the steps. Corrosion of earthing components may affect the effectiveness of the grounding system and increase the risk of static charge accumulation during solvent unloading operations.

2) The Earth-Rite static grounding system in the tank farm is not functioning. Solvent transfer without verified grounding can allow static charge to accumulate and ignite flammable vapors. Repair and test the system immediately, prevent transfer until grounding is confirmed, and include functional checks in the unloading checklist.
questions.recommendations:
1) Clean or replace the corroded earth plate, protect it with an approved corrosion-control method that does not insulate contact surfaces, and verify continuity and earth resistance. Label the point, record results, and include it in scheduled inspection and testing.

2) Stop solvent transfer until the Earth-Rite system is repaired and a valid ground is proven. Function-test the interlock and clamp, calibrate where applicable, include a pass/fail check in every unloading checklist, and retain preventive-maintenance records.

questions.observation:
1) No automatic fire modular or suppression system is provided for the capacitors located near the emergency exit in the PCC area. A capacitor fire could develop rapidly, produce smoke, and obstruct the evacuation route. Review the equipment location and fire load and provide suitable detection, suppression, segregation, and clear emergency-exit access.

2) A fire modular suppression unit is not provided in the UPS battery room near the IT department. An electrical or battery-related fire may spread before manual response is possible and can produce hazardous smoke or gases. Provide suitable detection and suppression based on the battery technology and fire risk assessment, with alarm integration and periodic testing.

3) Modular fire extinguisher was not available in the electrical panel room near the workshop. Absence of a suitable fire extinguisher in the electrical panel area may delay initial firefighting response and increase the risk of fire escalation during an electrical fault or short-circuit incident.
questions.recommendations:
1) Assess the capacitor-bank fire load and relocation options, then provide suitable automatic detection and suppression or certified compartmentation without obstructing the emergency exit. Integrate alarms, maintain required clearances, and conduct documented functional tests.

2) Assess the UPS battery technology and fire hazards and install compatible early detection and automatic suppression or other engineered protection. Provide ventilation and gas monitoring where required, integrate alarms, control ignition sources, and proof-test the system periodically.

3) Provide a suitable, approved extinguisher for energized electrical equipment at an accessible, clearly marked location outside the immediate hazard zone. Add it to the fire-equipment register and implement monthly inspection and scheduled competent-person servicing.

3) Provide approved snake-handling equipment in the Security Office and restrict use to trained designated responders. Establish a safe response procedure, emergency contact with an authorized wildlife or rescue service, equipment inspection, and incident reporting requirements.
